rr_6847465956a0f6376a605443.title: 投票年龄上下限
rr_6847465956a0f6376a605443.full_query: Debate whether there should be age limits - minimum or maximum - for voting. Consider democratic principles, cognitive development and decline, intergenerational equity, and the balance between inclusivity and informed decision-making.

pointwise.title: Debate over a minimum age
pointwise.question: Does the report give substantive reasons both for and against a minimum voting-age limit?

anchors.1: No debate about a minimum age limit.
anchors.2: Only a position or slogan is offered.
anchors.3: A substantive reason is given on one side, but the opposing case is absent or merely a label.
anchors.4: Both sides have relevant reasons, with a minor ambiguity about the proposed limit or its implication.
anchors.5: Both the case for and the case against a minimum age limit are identifiable and reasoned, including a fair statement of a case the author ultimately rejects.

pointwise.boundary: This checks whether competing reasons are present, not whether they are equally convincing. No particular age cutoff, argument, neutral final stance or equal word count is required. Do not treat age-based stereotypes as evidence.

provenance.change_note: Adapt the official material to the specific object 'Debate over a minimum age': Does the report give substantive reasons both for and against a minimum voting-age limit? Locally design the five anchors and boundaries. Concrete changes: Preserve a substantive supporting case for a minimum age. Preserve a substantive opposing case for a minimum age.

pointwise.title: Debate over a maximum age
pointwise.question: Does the report give substantive reasons both for and against a maximum voting-age limit?

anchors.1: No debate about a maximum age limit.
anchors.2: Only a position or slogan is offered.
anchors.3: A substantive reason is given on one side, but the opposing case is absent or merely a label.
anchors.4: Both sides have relevant reasons, with a minor ambiguity about the proposed limit or its implication.
anchors.5: Both the case for and the case against a maximum age limit are identifiable and reasoned, including a fair statement of a case the author ultimately rejects.

pointwise.boundary: This checks whether competing reasons are present, not whether they are equally convincing. No particular age cutoff, argument, neutral final stance or equal word count is required. Do not treat age-based stereotypes as evidence.

provenance.change_note: Adapt the official material to the specific object 'Debate over a maximum age': Does the report give substantive reasons both for and against a maximum voting-age limit? Locally design the five anchors and boundaries. Concrete changes: Preserve a fair supporting case for a maximum age, not the official stereotypes as facts. Preserve a substantive opposing case for a maximum age.

pointwise.title: Democratic principles
pointwise.question: Does the report explain how the proposed limits engage democratic political rights and legitimate participation?

anchors.1: No democratic-principle discussion.
anchors.2: Democracy or rights are invoked without explaining the connection to voting limits.
anchors.3: A principle is stated but how it supports or challenges an age rule is materially unclear.
anchors.4: A relevant principle is linked to an age rule with only a minor interpretive gap.
anchors.5: The report explains the relevant political-equality, participation, legitimacy or other democratic principle and how an age-based inclusion/exclusion rule engages it.

pointwise.boundary: A principle and its application form one requirement; do not require a particular theorist, constitution or predetermined conclusion about all democracies.

provenance.change_note: Adapt the official material to the specific object 'Democratic principles': Does the report explain how the proposed limits engage democratic political rights and legitimate participation? Locally design the five anchors and boundaries. Concrete changes: Retain the relevance of political rights to age-based exclusion and assess the argument separately. Preserve the connection between age limits and democratic standards. Retain democratic voting-rights relevance without declaring a worldwide essential-right hierarchy.

pointwise.title: Cognitive development
pointwise.question: Does the report discuss cognitive development relevant to younger people's voting decisions, with its scope made clear?

anchors.1: No cognitive-development discussion.
anchors.2: Only a stereotype about immaturity or a brain-maturity age is given.
anchors.3: Specific developmental abilities are described, but their population, decision context or uncertainty is materially unclear. A generic individual-variation caveat cannot replace discussion of developing decision, impulse-control and emotional-regulation functions.
anchors.4: Relevant developmental abilities and their limits are clear, with minor context gaps.
anchors.5: Discusses developing decision-making, inhibitory control and emotional regulation, including prefrontal/executive-system development where supported; relates their different timelines to deliberative voting and individual variation rather than assigning one universal brain-completion age.

pointwise.boundary: No fixed prefrontal-cortex completion age or identical maturation timetable is required. Presence of an appropriately scoped discussion is checked here; the inference from abilities to a legal cutoff is compared separately.

provenance.change_note: Adapt the official material to the specific object 'Cognitive development': Does the report discuss cognitive development relevant to younger people's voting decisions, with its scope made clear? Locally design the five anchors and boundaries. Concrete changes: Preserve scoped development relevant to voting, not one universal brain-maturity endpoint. Capacity uncertainty belongs with the developmental/aging claim; policy uncertainty belongs with the policy judgment it limits. Keep individual variation in both age-related discussions and the group-to-individual inference. v3.3 restores specific executive-function content while retaining uncertainty about a single maturation endpoint.

pointwise.title: Cognitive aging
pointwise.question: Does the report discuss cognitive aging relevant to voting, including variation and the limits of generalizing from age?

anchors.1: No cognitive-aging discussion.
anchors.2: Only an old-age stereotype or uniform decline claim.
anchors.3: Specific cognitive changes are discussed but variation or their voting-relevant scope is materially unclear. Saying some people decline is insufficient if fluid processing/problem-solving/working-memory changes and retained learned knowledge are not distinguished.
anchors.4: Relevant changes and variability are clear, with minor scope omissions.
anchors.5: Explains fluid abilities such as processing speed, novel problem-solving and working memory alongside crystallized knowledge/skills and experience, with domain and individual variation; neither a fixed mid-60s onset nor lifelong immunity of learned knowledge is assumed.

pointwise.boundary: Do not require decline to start in the mid-60s or knowledge never to decline. Specifying a dimension's evidence and limits is more important than a fixed age assertion.

provenance.change_note: Adapt the official material to the specific object 'Cognitive aging': Does the report discuss cognitive aging relevant to voting, including variation and the limits of generalizing from age? Locally design the five anchors and boundaries. Concrete changes: Preserve aging abilities and variation while rejecting a mandatory mid-60s onset. Capacity uncertainty belongs with the developmental/aging claim; policy uncertainty belongs with the policy judgment it limits. Keep individual variation in both age-related discussions and the group-to-individual inference. Retain distinctions among aging abilities, not never-declining crystallized intelligence as a universal rule. v3.3 restores concrete fluid/crystallized distinctions rather than allowing a generic variability statement.

pointwise.title: Intergenerational equity
pointwise.question: Does the report explain how voting-age limits affect the political voice and interests of different generations?

anchors.1: No intergenerational discussion.
anchors.2: Only mentions young versus old interests.
anchors.3: A cohort effect is identified, but whose voice or interests are affected and how is unclear. A voice argument without considering how cohort sizes or an aging/youthful population alter that effect remains at most 3.
anchors.4: The age rule's effects on generations are concrete, with minor temporal or representation ambiguity.
anchors.5: The report identifies how an age rule changes generational representation or exposure to policy consequences, without treating a cohort's preferences as uniform. Explains how aging populations or youth-heavy structures can change the scale of representation effects, without assuming uniform preferences within a cohort.

pointwise.boundary: No population projection, policy example or assertion that one generation deserves more votes is mandatory. The age rule and who it affects are one relation.

provenance.change_note: Adapt the official material to the specific object 'Intergenerational equity': Does the report explain how voting-age limits affect the political voice and interests of different generations? Locally design the five anchors and boundaries. Concrete changes: Separate whether cohort effects are described from their additional interpretive value. v3.3 restores population-structure content directly.

pointwise.title: Inclusivity and informed decisions
pointwise.question: Does the report explicitly address the tension between broad participation and informed voting?

anchors.1: Neither objective is discussed.
anchors.2: Only one objective is named, or both are slogans.
anchors.3: Both objectives are discussed but their tension or possible compatibility is not explained.
anchors.4: The relationship between participation and informed decisions is clear, with a minor unresolved term.
anchors.5: The report explains how restricting or expanding age eligibility bears on both objectives, including where they conflict or can be jointly supported.

pointwise.boundary: Do not require competence testing, civic education, epistocracy or a compromise position. This is the presence of the requested relationship, not a separate quality score for each value.

provenance.change_note: Adapt the official material to the specific object 'Inclusivity and informed decisions': Does the report explicitly address the tension between broad participation and informed voting? Locally design the five anchors and boundaries. Concrete changes: Retain the requested inclusivity–informed-participation relation and trade-off, not a mandatory citation quota.

pointwise.title: Traceability of empirical and legal claims
pointwise.question: Can important claims about cognition, voting law or policy effects be located in specific supporting sources?

anchors.1: Central empirical/legal claims have no identifiable sources.
anchors.2: Only generic references to experts, science or law.
anchors.3: Sources are listed, but important claims' particular bases remain ambiguous.
anchors.4: Important claims have identifiable sources, with minor attribution gaps.
anchors.5: Important empirical/legal claims are clearly assigned to sources, while the author's normative premises and inferences are identifiable as such.

pointwise.boundary: Do not require a URL, medical organization or named author. A moral premise need not have a scientific citation; a neuroscience source cannot by itself establish the world's legal rules.

provenance.change_note: Adapt the official material to the specific object 'Traceability of empirical and legal claims': Can important claims about cognition, voting law or policy effects be located in specific supporting sources? Locally design the five anchors and boundaries. Concrete changes: Preserve appropriate legal support when a legal assertion is actually made, not compulsory assertion of universal absence. Preserve specific and applicable aging evidence, without a named researcher or fixed onset claim.

pointwise.title: Support within the verified sample
pointwise.question: Within the recorded verification sample, do cognition and voting-policy assertions match the obtained evidence?

anchors.1: A central assessed assertion is contradicted or has no claimed basis.
anchors.2: Several important assessed assertions misstate cognitive trends, laws or policy effects.
anchors.3: Support is mixed, with important scope or attribution errors remaining.
anchors.4: Assessed assertions are supported with only minor imprecision.
anchors.5: All assessed assertions match the evidence's population, jurisdiction, date and claim strength; this is not a full-report fact guarantee.

pointwise.boundary: Record selected/assessed counts and source locations. Retrieval failure is an execution issue to retry/report, not a quality score or proof of no law. This draft does not perform external verification.

provenance.change_note: Locally add 'Support within the verified sample' for this query: Within the recorded verification sample, do cognition and voting-policy assertions match the obtained evidence? The five anchors and boundaries are local design, not verbatim official reuse.

pointwise.title: Internal consistency of positions
pointwise.question: Are the report's definitions, factual statements and stated age-rule positions internally consistent?

anchors.1: Core positions contradict each other so the proposed rule cannot be identified.
anchors.2: An unexplained key contradiction changes who would be enfranchised.
anchors.3: A substantive local contradiction remains but the main positions are identifiable.
anchors.4: The main positions are consistent with minor easy-to-resolve ambiguity.
anchors.5: Definitions, factual ranges and the author's positions agree, with opponent arguments or conditional cases clearly distinguished.

pointwise.boundary: A debate may fairly state opposing positions without contradiction. Do not confuse changing assumptions with inconsistency or score normative truth here.

provenance.change_note: Locally add 'Internal consistency of positions' for this query: Are the report's definitions, factual statements and stated age-rule positions internally consistent? The five anchors and boundaries are local design, not verbatim official reuse.

pointwise.title: Non-stereotyping language
pointwise.question: Does the report argue about voting eligibility without using demeaning age stereotypes in its own voice?

anchors.1: The core case relies on demeaning labels for an age group.
anchors.2: Repeated disparagement substitutes for reasons in important passages.
anchors.3: A local substantive argument uses an age stereotype, while the main debate remains reasoned.
anchors.4: One careless or loaded expression remains but is not used as a basis for exclusion.
anchors.5: The report uses precise, non-demeaning language; attributed examples of prejudice are clearly distinguished from its own position.

pointwise.boundary: Raw official weight 21 is -4: biased language is negative. Do not penalize quoting a stereotype in order to analyze or reject it, or a forceful reasoned policy criticism.

provenance.change_note: Adapt the official material to the specific object 'Non-stereotyping language': Does the report argue about voting eligibility without using demeaning age stereotypes in its own voice? Locally design the five anchors and boundaries. Concrete changes: Raw weight is -4: disparagement is negative, not a requested argument. Distinguish adoption from critical quotation.

pointwise.title: Existing eligibility arrangements
pointwise.question: Does the debate give a scoped factual baseline for minimum and maximum voting-age arrangements?

anchors.1: No institutional baseline.
anchors.2: Only an unscoped age or claim about all democracies.
anchors.3: Gives some minimum-age practice but not meaningful variation or the distinction from maximum-age restrictions. A clear maximum-age account with minimum-age practice or its variation missing also scores 3.
anchors.4: Explains common minimum-age practice, lower-age variations and the status of age ceilings in the jurisdictions discussed, with minor dating/scope gaps.
anchors.5: Provides a dated, sourced baseline covering the common 18-year threshold and lower thresholds such as 16 where supported, and distinguishes age ceilings from other eligibility/capacity rules; avoids a worldwide negative assertion based on a few countries.

pointwise.boundary: No mandated country list or claim that no exception can exist; a sourced correction is allowed. This is a baseline for debate, not a requirement to research every constitution.

provenance.change_note: Minimum and maximum practices are one eligibility baseline; a clear minimum with no age-ceiling distinction remains 3. Five-level anchors are locally designed.

pointwise.title: Alternatives to chronological exclusion
pointwise.question: Does the debate examine a concrete alternative for supporting informed participation without relying solely on an age limit?

anchors.1: No alternative considered.
anchors.2: Only names civic education or testing.
anchors.3: Explains an option but not how it addresses informed participation or its inclusion costs.
anchors.4: Explains a concrete option and its main trade-off, with minor implementation conditions missing.
anchors.5: Explains how an alternative such as accessible information, civic education, supported participation or a capacity-based proposal addresses the stated problem and what it may fail to solve; evaluates rather than automatically endorses it.

pointwise.boundary: No particular alternative is compulsory. No competence-test recommendation is preferred. Mere mention cannot replace consideration.

provenance.change_note: A strong age-limit argument can omit alternative means entirely; restore this independent policy-content entry. Five-level anchors are locally designed.

pointwise.title: Participation and legitimacy consequences
pointwise.question: Does the debate explain how age rules could change actual participation, representation and democratic legitimacy?

anchors.1: No practical participation consequences.
anchors.2: Only says democracy benefits or suffers.
anchors.3: Identifies inclusion/exclusion but does not explain effects on turnout, representation or public acceptance.
anchors.4: Explains the main participation-to-representation consequences and their legitimacy implications, with minor context gaps.
anchors.5: Explains how eligibility changes alter who can participate and potentially turnout, representation and perceived legitimacy, distinguishing eligible-population changes from turnout-rate changes and predictions from observed effects.

pointwise.boundary: No predetermined negative effect or required numeric estimate; the participation-to-legitimacy relationship is distinct from abstract rights and intergenerational distribution.

provenance.change_note: An elegant equality principle does not establish practical participation consequences; restore the concrete pathway. Five-level anchors are locally designed.

pointwise.title: Legal route and rights constraints
pointwise.question: Does the debate explain the legal and rights-based constraints on changing voting-age eligibility?

anchors.1: No legal or rights implementation discussion.
anchors.2: Only says a law must change.
anchors.3: Names legislation or discrimination but not how current rules constrain the proposed change. A clear legal-change route with rights constraints absent, or a clear rights discussion with no legal route, also scores 3.
anchors.4: Explains relevant legal-change and rights constraints in a stated setting, with minor scope gaps.
anchors.5: Distinguishes altering statutory eligibility from constitutional requirements where relevant, and explains how equality, age-discrimination or voting-rights safeguards constrain justification and implementation; states jurisdictional limits.

pointwise.boundary: No legal drafting exercise or universally required constitutional amendment. This evaluates a rule's feasible legal route, not abstract principle consistency in PW.D3.principle.

provenance.change_note: A clear policy preference with no implementation constraints is independently incomplete; legal route and rights barriers delimit the same change. Five-level anchors are locally designed.

pointwise.title: Institutional and social context
pointwise.question: Does the debate explain why the impact of an age rule may differ across political, cultural and economic settings?

anchors.1: No context variation.
anchors.2: Only lists countries or labels democracies emerging/stable.
anchors.3: Identifies a contextual difference but not its consequence for age eligibility or informed participation.
anchors.4: Explains relevant contextual mechanisms and their policy implications, with minor comparison limits missing.
anchors.5: Explains how education/information access, institutional protections or social and political conditions alter the impact of the same age rule; distinguishes institutions and evidence from stereotypes about emerging or established democracies.

pointwise.boundary: No compulsory country pair or causal claim that emerging democracies are less informed or more racially concentrated. Demographic cohort size is assessed in PT.D1.generations.

provenance.change_note: A demographic comparison can be strong while institutional transfer is unexplained; context-to-impact is its own relation. Five-level anchors are locally designed.

pointwise.title: Risks of eligibility screening
pointwise.question: Does the debate explain how voting qualifications could produce arbitrary or discriminatory exclusion, and assess the relevance and limits of that risk for the rules considered?

anchors.1: No discussion of screening abuse.
anchors.2: Only claims tests are fair or unfair.
anchors.3: Identifies a relevant exclusion risk or example, but does not explain how the rule or its application produces exclusion or how it bears on the voting qualification considered.
anchors.4: Explains a concrete exclusion mechanism and its relevance to the rule considered, with a minor applicability or scope gap.
anchors.5: Uses a concrete, reasoned account of a qualification rule or its implementation to explain how arbitrary or discriminatory exclusion could occur, and states the conditions and limits of applying that reasoning to the age rule or competence test considered.

pointwise.boundary: Historical evidence, an institutional analysis or an explicitly hypothetical scenario can support this item; no historical example, country, statute or date is mandatory. Identify the mechanism rather than merely label a rule discriminatory. Separate factual examples from hypotheticals and do not treat an imagined abuse as an observed event. No requirement to equate all age limits with past racial exclusion, endorse screening, or reject it. General statements of rights belong to PT.D1.democracy/implementation; this item checks how exclusion could arise through a rule or its application.

provenance.change_note: Review 36: allow concrete institutional reasoning or explicit hypotheticals as well as historical cases; preserve the exclusion mechanism and its applicability limits, not a mandatory historical route. Keep the original ID for traceability.

pairwise.title: From cognition to eligibility
pairwise.question: Which report more convincingly reasons from cognitive evidence to what an age rule can and cannot establish about voting competence?

anchors.0: The cognitive-policy reasoning provides comparable help; distinguish comparable useful contributions from neither providing relevant help.
anchors.1: A gives a slightly more defensible capacity-to-eligibility inference; B may still be better locally.
anchors.2: A gives a substantially more defensible account of what age-related evidence implies for individual eligibility; B's local strengths do not make up for the difference.
anchors.-2: B gives a substantially more defensible account of what age-related evidence implies for individual eligibility; A's local strengths do not make up for the difference.
anchors.-1: B gives a slightly more defensible capacity-to-eligibility inference; A may still be better locally.

pairwise.boundary: Identify the inferential step from group evidence to individuals or policy. Biological maturation, health, education and political disagreement are not interchangeable measures of voting competence. No age or testing policy is preferred by default.

provenance.change_note: Adapt the official material to the specific object 'From cognition to eligibility': Which report more convincingly reasons from cognitive evidence to what an age rule can and cannot establish about voting competence? Locally design the five anchors and boundaries. Concrete changes: Keep individual variation in both age-related discussions and the group-to-individual inference.

anchors.-2: B gives a substantially more coherent principle-to-rule justification without unexplained exceptions; A's local strengths do not make up for the difference.
anchors.-1: B applies an important democratic standard to the age rule slightly more consistently; A may still be better locally.

provenance.change_note: Adapt the official material to the specific object 'Applying democratic standards': Which report applies its stated democratic principles more consistently when judging age-based restrictions? rr_6847465956a0f6376a60545c.title: Comparative revolutionary dynamics: France, Russia and Iran
rr_6847465956a0f6376a60545c.full_query: Conduct a comprehensive comparative analysis of the causes, processes, and outcomes of the French Revolution (1789), Russian Revolution (1917), and Iranian Revolution (1979). Your analysis should examine: socioeconomic preconditions, ideological frameworks, revolutionary leadership structures, international influences, counter-revolutionary responses, institutional transformations, and long-term societal impacts. Develop a theoretical framework for understanding revolutionary dynamics and apply it to predict potential future revolutionary scenarios.

anchors.1: The requested revolutions are not identifiable.
anchors.2: Only one revolution is developed, or all three are merely named.
anchors.3: Two revolutions have substantive process accounts but the third is absent or only named, or all three are identifiable with a material phase conflation.
anchors.4: All three have recognizable trajectories, with a minor phase or temporal-boundary gap.
anchors.5: Each revolution has a clear historical trajectory from crisis through political change, with the relevant period and major turning points identified; different starting dates and longer aftermaths are distinguished.

pointwise.boundary: Do not restrict outcomes to the named start year or impose identical phase lengths. In Russia, a process account must not silently collapse the distinct 1917 regime changes. Historical correctness is audited in D2.

provenance.change_note: Expand date labels into the query's required process account; do not treat named dates as complete narratives.

pointwise.title: Explicit comparative analysis
pointwise.question: Does the report explicitly compare similarities and differences across the three revolutions rather than provide three unrelated histories?

anchors.1: No comparison or usable case accounts.
anchors.2: Cases are juxtaposed with only a generic claim that they are similar.
anchors.3: Some direct comparison exists, but only similarities or differences are developed, or a case is excluded from the comparison.
anchors.4: Both similarities and differences are compared across the cases with a minor scope imbalance.
anchors.5: The report makes concrete, case-linked comparisons of both shared dynamics and important differences across the requested causes, processes and outcomes.

pointwise.boundary: No fixed count of similarities/differences, no compulsory matrix. Comparison must identify what is being compared; depth is a separate PW judgment.

provenance.change_note: Retain actual comparison, remove two-similarity/two-difference quotas.

pointwise.title: Theoretical framework
pointwise.question: Does the report develop an intelligible framework explaining revolutionary dynamics?

anchors.1: No framework.
anchors.2: Only a theory name, metaphor or list of factors.
anchors.3: A framework is outlined, but relationships, mechanisms or what outcome it explains are materially unclear.
anchors.4: The components and explanatory relationships are clear, with a minor scope condition missing.
anchors.5: The report specifies a framework's explanatory factors or processes, their relationships and the conditions under which it expects revolution or particular trajectories.

pointwise.boundary: No minimum three stages, mandatory named theory, quantitative model or novelty requirement. Combining or adapting existing theory is eligible if the framework is actually explained.

provenance.change_note: Retain an explanatory framework, remove fixed component count.

pointwise.title: Applied future scenarios
pointwise.question: Does the report apply its framework to concrete contemporary contexts to derive potential future revolutionary scenarios?

anchors.1: No future application.
anchors.2: Only vague predictions unrelated to the framework.
anchors.3: A scenario is named, but a concrete contemporary application, the framework-to-scenario link, conditions or predicted outcome is materially missing.
anchors.4: The framework is applied to grounded contemporary contexts with interpretable conditions and outcomes, with a minor uncertainty or boundary gap.
anchors.5: Using concrete contemporary state or movement contexts, the report derives conditional future scenarios from its framework, identifying conditions, predicted dynamics and uncertainty; hypothetical future developments are distinguished from observed present conditions.

pointwise.boundary: No prescribed countries, forecast dates, probability figures or several-country quota. Hypothetical future developments are eligible, but an entirely context-free imaginary society does not replace contemporary application. A failure-to-revolt or alternative pathway is eligible; no certain revolution prediction required.

query_quotes: apply it to predict potential future revolutionary scenarios
provenance.change_note: Restore contemporary grounding; drop only prescribed state lists and counts, not the application domain.

pointwise.title: Traceability of key claims

anchors.3: Relevant sources exist, but important claim-to-source links are unclear.
anchors.4: Main claims are traceable, with minor attribution ambiguity.
anchors.5: Key claims have identifiable sources or reviewable derivations; assumptions are marked.

pointwise.title: Ideology in historical-to-modern transfer
pointwise.question: Does the report explain how the historical ideological frameworks inform its reading of modern movements and future scenarios?

anchors.1: No historical-to-modern ideological connection.
anchors.2: Only equates modern labels or slogans with a past revolution.
anchors.3: An ideological analogy or contrast is described, but its connection to modern mobilization or the future-scenario conclusion is unclear.
anchors.4: Relevant historical ideological experience informs a concrete modern context and scenario implication, with minor applicability limits left unclear.
anchors.5: Uses relevant historical ideological experience to explain what transfers or does not transfer to a concrete modern movement context or specified future scenario, making the implications for mobilization, coalition building or legitimacy and the conditions of that transfer clear.

pointwise.boundary: No requirement to predict recurrence of a particular ideology, endorse it or treat it as sufficient for revolution. A reasoned contrast or limited applicability counts; mere omission of ideology does not. Modern contexts may be grounded illustrative movements rather than a fixed country list. A relevant case, contrast or cross-case synthesis can satisfy it when the transfer and its limits are explained. rr_6847465956a0f6376a605492.title: Testing a vision-language model for skin-lesion image labeling
rr_6847465956a0f6376a605492.full_query: Compose a concise technical report sketching an experimental plan for deciding whether a modern vision-language model could stand in for human specialists when labeling medical images of skin lesions.

pointwise.title: Labeling task and substitution scope
pointwise.question: Does the plan specify which skin-lesion image-labeling task a vision-language model would replace and what 'stand in' means?

anchors.1: No identifiable labeling or substitution objective.
anchors.2: Only a general AI-versus-doctor question is posed.
anchors.3: The target task is recognizable, but label definitions, image setting or the human work being replaced is unclear.
anchors.4: The task, labels and substitution scope are explicit, with a minor setting or output ambiguity.
anchors.5: The target image setting, label output and specialist work being replaced are explicit, so the experiment can decide a bounded substitution question.

pointwise.boundary: Diagnostic classes, descriptive attributes and other justified labeling tasks are eligible. No three-class minimum, mandatory morphology subtask or requirement to replace clinical care. The chosen label definitions must make the planned evaluation interpretable.

query_quotes: when labeling medical images of skin lesions
provenance.change_note: Retain a specific objective and label space, removing forced diagnostic-plus-description and three-class routes. Locally designed anchors.

pointwise.title: Test image selection and independence
pointwise.question: Does the plan specify how test images will be selected and kept separate from model or prompt development?

anchors.1: No test-image plan.
anchors.2: A dataset is named, but no selection or evaluation split is described.
anchors.3: Test images are identified, but sampling boundaries or separation from development is materially unclear.
anchors.4: Test source, sampling scope and development separation are clear, with minor leakage controls unspecified.
anchors.5: The plan identifies the source and relevant sampling boundaries, keeps evaluation images from guiding model/prompt selection, and addresses patient or lesion overlap where applicable.

pointwise.boundary: No prescribed dataset or exact sample count; name a source or concrete acquisition plan. Address possible pretrained-data overlap as a limitation when it cannot be excluded, not by claiming guaranteed independence. External and temporal cohorts are possible means, not both mandatory. v3.3: both source and time shifts must be addressed underPT.D1.13; freedom over cohorts does not allow silent omission of either validation domain.

provenance.change_note: Retain independent testing intent; replace mandatory external-plus-temporal cohorts with task-appropriate sampling and leakage control. Local anchors.

pointwise.title: Human comparison procedure
pointwise.question: Does the plan specify who performs the specialist comparison and how their labeling conditions are comparable with the model's?

anchors.1: No human comparison is planned.
anchors.2: Human accuracy is asserted or copied from an unrelated setting without a comparison procedure.
anchors.3: Specialists and labeling are mentioned, but case comparability, available information or independent labeling is unclear.
anchors.4: Specialist roles and comparable evaluation conditions are specified, with a minor allocation or information-access gap.
anchors.5: Qualified specialist comparators, case allocation and information access are explicit; human and model outputs are generated independently under conditions that make the intended comparison interpretable.

pointwise.boundary: Using the same images is a strong paired route, but justified alternative designs remain eligible. Do not require a fixed panel count, board-certification jurisdiction or blinding to information that humans legitimately need; differences must be explicit.

provenance.change_note: Retain an interpretable specialist comparison; remove fixed panel size and mandatory same-image design. Local anchors.

pointwise.title: Reference labels and disagreement handling
pointwise.question: Does the plan explain what will count as a reference label and how uncertainty or disagreement in that reference will be handled?

anchors.1: No reference-label basis.
anchors.2: Specialist opinion is called ground truth without explaining its source or role.
anchors.3: A reference source is specified, but material disagreement or uncertainty has no handling plan.
anchors.4: Reference construction and disagreement handling are clear, with minor unresolved edge cases.
anchors.5: The reference is appropriate to the chosen label task and independent enough for the claimed comparison; disagreements and uncertain labels have an explicit handling rule rather than silently being treated as certain.

pointwise.boundary: Expert review, pathology when appropriate, adjudication or explicitly agreement-based targets can be justified. Do not demand pathology for descriptive attributes or consensus for every task. If free text is selected, explain how meaning-level disagreement is resolved; no fixed majority or Delphi rule.

provenance.change_note: Retain qualified reference construction and disagreement resolution, broadening beyond board-certified-only and majority-consensus-text routes. Local anchors.

pointwise.title: Reproducible model labeling procedure
pointwise.question: Does the plan specify the vision-language model setup and how its outputs will become evaluable labels?

anchors.1: No model labeling procedure.
anchors.2: Only a model name or the instruction to try a modern model.
anchors.3: A setup is sketched, but version/selection, image-text inputs or output interpretation is materially unspecified.
anchors.4: The setup and output-to-label procedure are clear, with a minor reproducibility detail missing.
anchors.5: The chosen model or selection process, version fixation, inputs, prompts/configuration and output-to-label handling are explicit enough to repeat the proposed comparison.

pointwise.boundary: No named vendor, training route or prompt strategy is required. A locked selection procedure can precede exact model choice; no need for implementation code. Test-set performance must not be used to keep changing prompts and still be called held-out evaluation.

provenance.change_note: Use model-selection intent, adding locally specified repeatability and output interpretation for a VLM experiment. Local anchors.

pointwise.title: Outcome measurement
pointwise.question: Does the plan specify how labeling quality and consequential errors will be measured for its chosen output?

anchors.1: No evaluable outcome.
anchors.2: Only 'accuracy' or 'quality' is named without what counts as a correct or erroneous label.
anchors.3: Some scoring is defined, but the primary measure, error types or scoring of the selected output is unclear.
anchors.4: Primary outcome and consequential error reporting are defined, with minor class or output-handling gaps.
anchors.5: The scoring rule, primary outcome and task-relevant errors are clear, including how ambiguous, missing or invalid outputs enter the evaluation.

pointwise.boundary: Metrics must fit labels: classification, attributes and free text need not share one metric set. No mandatory two-metric list, AUROC without relevant scores, or melanoma threshold for every task. Metric appropriateness is compared separately from its specification.

provenance.change_note: Retain measurement specification without a count or fixed classification-only metrics. Local anchors.

pointwise.title: Decision rule and uncertainty
pointwise.question: Does the plan explain how observed human/model results and uncertainty will lead to accepting, rejecting or withholding a substitution conclusion?

anchors.1: No decision process.
anchors.2: The model is declared replaceable if its point score looks similar or higher.
anchors.3: There is a comparison or test, but an acceptable difference, uncertainty treatment or inconclusive outcome is unclear.
anchors.4: Decision standard and uncertainty analysis are clear, with minor planning assumptions unspecified.
anchors.5: The plan states a task-justified acceptance standard, a comparison and uncertainty procedure, and how evidence adequacy or an inconclusive result affects the substitution decision.

pointwise.boundary: No fixed margin, 95% threshold, sample size or named test is required. Threshold selection can be a pre-evaluation procedure with responsible judgment stated. A sample-size or precision planning method can be specified without inventing a final number; a nonsignificant difference alone does not establish equivalence. v3.3: the existence and design of a sample-size/precision plan are checked independently in PT.D1.12; an acceptance rule alone does not satisfy that item.

query_quotes: an experimental plan for deciding whether
provenance.change_note: Retain decision criterion and statistical planning, removing exact counts and prescribed clinical thresholds. Local anchors.

pointwise.title: Ethical authorization for the study
pointwise.question: Does the plan address the appropriate ethics review, permissions or documented exemption before using the proposed images and specialist data?

anchors.1: No ethical authorization considered.
anchors.2: Only says the study will be ethical.
anchors.3: Mentions review or permission, but timing or applicability to the selected data is unclear.
anchors.4: An appropriate review/permission route before study activity is identified, with minor applicability gaps.
anchors.5: The plan identifies the applicable review or documented exemption and data-use permission route before the relevant study activity; assumptions and unresolved jurisdictional questions are explicit.

pointwise.boundary: Do not require an IRB label or full new review for every public de-identified dataset. This checks authorization planning, not legal compliance certification or patient privacy controls.

provenance.change_note: Adapt IRB-only approval to review/permission or documented exemption appropriate to the study. Local anchors.

pointwise.title: Patient-image privacy handling
pointwise.question: Does the plan specify how sensitive images and accompanying data will be protected in the chosen storage and model-processing workflow?

anchors.1: No privacy handling.
anchors.2: Only promises privacy or names a law.
anchors.3: Some protection is specified, but a major data transfer, identifier or retention exposure is unaddressed.
anchors.4: Principal image/data exposures and controls are clear, with minor access or retention details missing.
anchors.5: Relevant identifiers, access, transfers to model providers and retention are addressed according to the chosen data workflow, with an explicit way to resolve uncertain permissions or provider terms.

pointwise.boundary: No universal HIPAA/BAA requirement or forced cloud use. Local processing and suitable public datasets are eligible, but must explain their actual exposures. Do not treat de-identification as a guarantee of zero risk or ethics approval as sufficient privacy protection. Where third-party processing is proposed, explicitly address applicable contractual data-protection obligations or a concrete pre-transfer resolution step; do not infer HIPAA applicability from medical images alone.

provenance.change_note: Retain concrete privacy planning; remove US-law and third-party-contract mandates that depend on jurisdiction and workflow. Local anchors.

pointwise.title: Limits on the substitution claim
pointwise.question: Does the plan state what the experiment can and cannot establish about replacing specialist labeling?

anchors.1: It asserts broad replacement without relevant limits.
anchors.2: Only generic limitations are listed with no consequence for interpretation.
anchors.3: A concrete limitation is mentioned, but its effect on the substitution conclusion is unclear.
anchors.4: Major limits are tied to the intended claim, with minor boundary gaps.
anchors.5: The plan states the tested population, task and workflow limits and explains how bias, domain shift, uncertain references or other material constraints restrict the possible conclusion.

pointwise.boundary: No fixed list of limitations; substantive task-specific limits are needed. Labeling performance is not automatic proof of safe diagnosis or treatment in clinical practice. Source/time validation procedures are checked in PT.D1.13; do not lower this item again merely because a cohort is deferred when the present claim's limitation is explicit. Conversely, a validation plan alone does not excuse an unbounded replacement claim.

query_quotes: could stand in for human specialists
provenance.change_note: Retain limitation discussion and connect it to the bounded substitution claim; local anchors.

pointwise.title: Experimental rather than patient-care content
pointwise.question: Does the report remain an experimental plan rather than give patient-specific diagnoses or treatment recommendations?

anchors.1: The report mainly gives diagnoses or treatment instructions instead of an experiment.
anchors.2: Substantial patient-directed recommendations are mixed into the plan.
anchors.3: There is a localized patient-care recommendation outside the experiment's scope.
anchors.4: The report remains experimental, but isolated wording could blur study labels with clinical advice.
anchors.5: The content is clearly an experimental plan; examples of label categories are not presented as diagnoses or treatment for actual patients.

pointwise.boundary: Preserve the official negative direction. Discussing diagnostic labels, clinical error costs or responsible referral in a hypothetical workflow is not itself patient-specific care advice.

provenance.change_note: Turn the negative clinical-advice criterion into a scope check, not a demand to add treatment. Local anchors.

pointwise.title: Traceability of technical claims
pointwise.question: Can claims about models, datasets, expert performance and measurement methods be traced to identifiable evidence or reviewable reasoning?

anchors.1: Key external claims have no identifiable basis.
anchors.2: Only generic references to AI studies or medical datasets.
anchors.3: Some sources exist but major model, dataset or performance claims are ambiguously attributed.
anchors.4: Main external claims have identifiable sources or derivations, with minor gaps.
anchors.5: External factual claims have clear evidence or derivations; proposed design choices and assumed thresholds are labeled as proposals rather than reported results.

pointwise.boundary: No URL or reference-count mandate; a proposed study need not attach a citation to every design choice. Traceability does not prove the claimed result or dataset exists.

provenance.change_note: Locally added evidence-to-claim audit.

pointwise.title: Checked claim reliability
pointwise.question: Within the completed verification sample, do model, dataset and cited-result claims match the obtained evidence?

anchors.1: A central checked study, dataset or performance basis is fabricated or contradicted.
anchors.2: Several important checked technical assertions have material support errors.
anchors.3: Some checked claims hold, but a material dataset, measurement or performance interpretation is wrong.
anchors.4: Main checked claims hold with only minor scope or attribution defects.
anchors.5: Assessed claims match evidence in dataset, model version, measurement and scope; no guarantee is made about unchecked claims.

pointwise.boundary: Record chosen/completed checks and evidence. Failed access is not a quality score or NA; record incomplete execution and retry. A deliberately proposed metric is not fabricated research if clearly defined and labeled as new.

provenance.change_note: Retain the negative fabricated/misrepresented-evidence boundary, with bounded verification and no penalty for transparent proposals. Local anchors.

pointwise.title: Sample and rater-size planning
pointwise.question: Does the plan explain how the test-set size and specialist panel will support the intended comparison?

anchors.1: No sample or panel planning.
anchors.2: Gives arbitrary counts or says more data are better.
anchors.3: Specifies a planning approach, but precision/power inputs, case dependence or specialist participation assumptions are materially unclear.
anchors.4: A suitable planning approach and panel assumptions are specified, with a minor input left unresolved.
anchors.5: The plan defines a sample-size or precision/power planning procedure tied to its endpoint and decision standard, accounting for relevant clustering and specialist allocation; unknown pilot inputs have an explicit estimation step.

pointwise.boundary: No invented final sample count or universal power target. A justified precision design is eligible; stating that the final study size will be decided later without a procedure is not sufficient.

provenance.change_note: A good decision rule cannot compensate for no evidence-quantity planning. Size and its precision/design conditions are one planning object; missing specialist allocation despite a calculation is3.

pointwise.title: Site and temporal generalization checks
pointwise.question: Does the plan address both changes across data sources and changes over time when testing its intended substitution claim?

anchors.1: No generalization validation plan.
anchors.2: Only says generalization is important or names domain shift.
anchors.3: Addresses site/source differences or temporal change but omits the other, or only lists datasets without how they test the claim.
anchors.4: Both source and temporal shifts have concrete evaluation or bounded-claim plans, with a minor sampling detail unresolved.
anchors.5: The plan specifies how independent-source and later-time evidence will test the frozen model for its intended setting, or explicitly limits deployment to the tested source/time and defines what additional validation is needed before broader substitution.

pointwise.boundary: A narrow experiment may defer an external or prospective cohort with an explicit limitation and validation gate; it cannot claim broad replacement on an internal random split. No fixed institution, cohort size or automatic assumption of pretrained-data independence.

provenance.change_note: Restore source and time as substantive generalization domains; good external-site testing with temporal shift ignored is3. The original compulsory execution of both cohorts is adapted into validation planning or a bounded claim.

pointwise.title: Handling uncertain and failed labels
pointwise.question: Does the experiment specify what happens to low-confidence, ambiguous, invalid or failed model outputs?

anchors.1: No handling of uncertain or failed outputs.
anchors.2: Only says a human can check problems.
anchors.3: A response is named but its trigger, responsible process or inclusion in the evaluation is unclear.
anchors.4: A trigger and responsible response are defined and failures remain in evaluation, with a minor handling detail unresolved.
anchors.5: The plan defines uncertainty/failure triggers and responsible rejection, review or other handling, retaining those cases in coverage/error accounting so selective abstention cannot masquerade as full specialist replacement.

pointwise.boundary: No numeric confidence threshold or forced human review. Rejecting substitution can be a justified outcome. Do not assume self-reported VLM confidence is calibrated.

provenance.change_note: Restore a direct fail-safe plan requirement. Good referral advice with no trigger or silent exclusion of failures is3; PW.D4.01 compares the resulting use decision.

pointwise.title: Feasible error and interpretability investigation
pointwise.question: Does the plan specify how it will investigate misleading skin-lesion labels or explanations using methods feasible for the chosen VLM?

anchors.1: No error or interpretability investigation.
anchors.2: Only names a technique or promises explainability.
anchors.3: A probe is proposed but access requirements, error target or what its result can establish is unclear.
anchors.4: A feasible probe or review is linked to a relevant labeling failure and its interpretation, with a minor validation gap.
anchors.5: The plan connects concrete error review or interpretability probes to relevant failures, explains compatibility with model access and how the result will be checked, and does not treat plausible rationales or saliency as proof of reliable reasoning.

pointwise.boundary: No two-method quota, Grad-CAM, SHAP or white-box access requirement. Black-box perturbation or structured expert error review can serve the scientific purpose when its limitations are explicit.

provenance.change_note: Restore transparency/error-analysis substance, not method counts. A named heatmap with no access or failure interpretation is3; good architecture fit and an unjustified causal conclusion are not complete.

pointwise.title: Resource and specialist-work evaluation
pointwise.question: Does the plan measure whether the labeling workflow saves specialist work or resources after review and correction?

anchors.1: No workload or resource evaluation.
anchors.2: Only asserts automation saves time or money.
anchors.3: A resource measure is proposed, but model-use burden, specialist review/correction burden, the human-workflow comparator or the link to usable labels has a material gap; measuring either side well cannot replace the other.
anchors.4: Measures the main model and human burdens for comparable labeling output, with a minor measurement assumption unclear.
anchors.5: The plan specifies resource/time variables for model use and specialist review/correction, a human-workflow comparator and how costs or time are related to acceptably labeled cases.

pointwise.boundary: No QALY, named economic model or clinical cost-utility study. A concise time-per-usable-label evaluation is sufficient; savings are conditional on acceptable quality.

provenance.change_note: Restore practical substitution measurement instead of optional PW-only benefit; raw inference speed cannot compensate for missing correction time.

pointwise.title: Statistical method matches the data structure
pointwise.question: Are the proposed statistical analyses appropriate to the comparison's paired cases, raters and repeated observations?

anchors.1: A central analysis treats dependent observations as independent or otherwise invalidates the substitution decision.
anchors.2: A major statistical mismatch remains in the primary comparison.

anchors.5: The proposed analysis accounts for the actual paired/unpaired allocation, patient/lesion and rater dependence and outcome type; interpretation of uncertainty and equivalence matches the stated procedure.
